notes.wange: Agrees with people nouns (mu-/ba- class, singular): maama wange, my mother.
notes.oluganda: The language. A Muganda person speaks Oluganda.

guidebook.intro: This unit introduces people, things and your first verbs, and with them the idea that drives Luganda grammar: noun classes.

tips.title: Noun classes
body: Every Luganda noun belongs to a class, shown by its prefix. Classes come in singular and plural pairs. People usually take **omu-** in the singular and **aba-** in the plural; many things take **eki-** and **ebi-**.

Words that go with a noun change to match its class. “My” is **wange** with one person, **bange** with people, **kyange** with an **eki-** thing and **byange** with **ebi-** things. You met another one in Unit 1: **erinnya lyange**, my name.

tips.title: The first vowel comes and goes
body: Most nouns start with a vowel: **o**muyizi, **e**kitabo, **a**baana. This initial vowel drops in some places, for example after “I am”: **Ndi muyizi** (I am a student), or when the noun describes something: **Abaana bayizi** (the children are students).
Family words like **maama**, **taata** and **jjajja** have no prefix and don’t change.

tips.title: Who does it: n- and o-
body: Verbs show who is acting with a prefix. **n-** means “I” and **o-** means “you” (one person). The verb stem stays the same.

culture.title: Family is wide
body: Kinship words cover more people than in English. Your father’s brothers are also **taata**, and your mother’s sisters are also **maama**. Your father’s sister is your **ssenga** and your mother’s brother your **kojja**.
**Jjajja** means grandparent, and it is a warm, respectful way to address any elder.

culture.title: Oluganda, Muganda, Buganda
body: The same root gives many words: **Oluganda** is the language, a **Muganda** is one person of the Baganda people, and **Buganda** is their kingdom in central Uganda.
